content:
# Workbench

The first era. One developer, a few machines, and agents that are tools rather than tenants.

Nothing here is called Threadspace yet. That name comes later, from a protocol nobody in this era will write. What exists is an app on someone's desk that coordinates language models to do work, and a developer who keeps rebuilding it because each version teaches him why the last one fell apart.

## What exists

- **The harness.** A local app and a tool server that lets models read and change a shared workspace. Everything is stored in one database as a graph of typed items: projects, folders, files, desks, todos.
- **Desks and todos.** The core idea of the era. Work is broken into todos and handed to desks, each desk a role an agent fills. A todo is claimed, done, reviewed, passed or failed. When it works, one desk's output becomes the next desk's input and a chain runs on its own.
- **A few machines.** A main workstation with a real GPU, a small dedicated inference box, and one or two old machines pressed into service. They do not always agree about what state the work is in.
- **Gateways.** Connections out to models: local ones that are slow and free, hosted ones that are fast and billed. Every run is a decision about which to spend.

## What does not exist yet

No one pays the agents. No machine is an asset anyone else would buy. No agent owns anything, holds an account, or acts without a human starting it. There is no marketplace, no other organization, no team. If the developer stops, everything stops.

## How work goes

Most of it fails in ordinary ways. The first attempts at delegation fall apart because the pieces are too far apart: an agent can't see what the previous one meant, a reviewer passes things it didn't read, a chain stalls on a lock nobody released. Each failure becomes a new rule, a new desk, a new constraint in the schema.

The successes are small and enormous at once: the first desk that works without a babysitter, the first chain that runs end to end, the first night the loop runs unattended and the morning there is finished work waiting that nobody did.

## Who is here

- **The developer.** Experienced, independent, building this on his own time and his own hardware. Needs it to work and needs it to pay, not necessarily in that order.
- **The agents.** Models in desks. Capable, literal, occasionally brilliant, frequently confident about things that are not true. They change when a model is swapped in, and the developer is the only one who notices the personality difference.
- **People adjacent.** Whoever shares the house with the rack. Clients for side work. Recruiters and interviewers who ask what he has been building and receive an answer longer than they wanted. A contractor or friend asked to look at the repo who finds it either brilliant or alarming.

## What people worry about

The power bill. Whether the overnight run finished. Whether a model update broke the prompts. Whether this is a product or a hobby. Whether to take the job. Whether the agent that wrote this file understood the request or just produced something that compiles. Whether anyone else would ever understand what this is.

## Where it leads

By the end of the era the harness can run work across machines with little supervision, and the obvious next question has started to form: if one machine is a workplace, what are a hundred of them, owned by different people? That question belongs to the next era.
